question.text:
Independent variables satisfy X ∼ N(2, 9) and Y ∼ N (−1, 4). In terms of the standard normal
CDF, what is P(X + 2Y > 5)?
√
(A) 1 − Φ(1) (B) 1 − Φ(5/7) (C) 1 − Φ(5/ 17) (D) Φ(1) (E) 1 − Φ(5/13)

solution.text:
The mean of X +2Y is 2+2(−1) = 0, and its variance is 9+4(4) = 25. Its standard deviation
is 5, so the standardized threshold is 5/5 = 1.

For X ∼ N(µ, σ ) with σ > 0, suppose P(X ≤ 4) = Φ(−1) and P (X ≤ 10) = Φ(2). What is
µ + σ?
(A) 6 (B) 7 (C) 8 (D) 9 (E) 10

solution.text:
Strict increase of Φ gives (4 − µ)/σ = −1 and (10 − µ)/σ = 2. Subtracting yields 6 = 3σ, so
σ = 2 and µ = 6. Hence µ + σ = 8.

question.text:
For a standard normal variable Z, what is P(|Z| > 2 | |Z| > 1)?
1 − Φ(2) Φ(2) − Φ(1) 1 − Φ(1)
(A) 1 − Φ(2) (B) 2[1 − Φ(2)] (C) (D) (E)
1 − Φ(1) 1 − Φ(1) 1 − Φ(2)

solution.text:
The event |Z| > 2 is contained in |Z| > 1, so conditional probability is their probability ra-
tio. Symmetry gives tail probabilities 2[1 − Φ(2)] and 2[1 − Φ(1)]; the factors of two cancel.
The ratio is approximately 0.0228/0.1587 ≈ 0.144.

question.text:
Let X ∼ N(3, 4), with the second parameter denoting variance. Which pair gives the real a
maximizing P (a ≤ X ≤ a + 4) and that maximum probability?
(A) (1, 2Φ(1) − 1) (B) (3, Φ(2) − 1/2)
(C) (1, 2Φ(2) − 1) (D) (−1, 2Φ(1) − 1)
(E) (3, 2Φ(1) − 1)

solution.text:
The interval must be centered at the mean 3, so a = 1. More explicitly, the derivative of
the interval probability is f (a + 4) − f (a), positive for a < 1 and negative for a > 1 by
the symmetric unimodal density. The optimal interval [1, 5] lies one standard deviation on
either side of the mean, giving Φ(1) − Φ(−1) = 2Φ(1) − 1.
